newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Euro MP demands Britain pay for BSE damage.
newsitem.headline: Euro MP demands Britain pay for BSE damage.

text.p: The European Commission should consider asking the European Court of Justice to make Britain compensate its EU partners for losses due to the mad cow crisis, the author of a European Parliament report said on Friday.

In provisional conclusions, Spanish Socialist Manuel Medina blamed Britain for failing to take necessary safety measures to tackle the disease, known as Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE), since it emerged in Britain in 1986.

"In view of the massive economic damage done to the EU by the BSE crisis, the Commission should investigate the possibility of appealing to the Court of Justice to rule on the extent of the UK's liability," said Medina, an international lawyer.

An announcement by Britain's conservative government in March that BSE could possibly be passed to humans who ate infected beef triggered a fresh wave of consumer panic and a sharp drop in beef sales.

The EU agreed this summer to 850 million Ecus ($1.1 billion) emergency aid for stricken cattle producers across Europe as well as to help fund the annual slaughtering of one million older British cattle a year.
Commission chief spokesman Nikolaus van der Pas declined comment on possible court action.
"It's an interesting and too important a matter to improvise upon," he told a news briefing.
Medina, leader of Spain's socialist Euro MPs, also attacked the EU's executive Commission for adopting a "minimalistic" approach to the crisis.

"The Commission's activities have been limited to adopting a precaution recommended by the veterinary scientific committees without putting forward further measures providing greater guarantees for the health and safety of consumers," he said.

The European Parliament, which set up a committee of inquiry into BSE in July, has heard evidence from EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler, Commission Director General for Agriculture Guy Legras as well as officials and experts from member states.
British agriculture minister Douglas Hogg declined to attend but was represented this week by the ministry's permanent secretary Richard Packer.
The committee is due to wind up its work on November 12.
